title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbook Standards
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview:

This page consolidates SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning guidance, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling recommendations, and runbook templates used by Redwood Inference. The goal is to provide a single, actionable reference for service owners and on-call engineers to ensure predictable reliability and efficient capacity economics across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Scope and audience:
- Applies to production-facing services in the inference stack: api-generation, streaming-proxy, batcher, kv-cache, model-router, telemetry-ingest.
- Primary audience: service owners, SREs, on-call engineers, and platform engineers.

1) SLO and Error Budget Standards

Principles:
- Every production service must have at least one availability SLO and one key-transaction latency SLO where applicable.
- SLOs should reflect user-facing impact. For internal-only infra (e.g., ETL pipelines), choose durability/throughput SLOs instead.
- Keep SLOs simple and measurable using existing telemetry (Prometheus, Cortex/Thanos, and Datadog for traces).

Required SLOs (recommended defaults):
| Service class | Availability SLO | Latency SLO (P95) | Rationale |
|---------------|------------------|-------------------|-----------|
| User-facing generation (api-generation) | 99.95% monthly | < 300 ms | Strong UX requirement for interactive latency |
| Streaming responses (streaming-proxy) | 99.9% monthly | median < 150 ms | Streaming critical for UX; focus on tail behavior separately |
| Background batching (batcher) | 99.9% monthly | 99% jobs complete within SLA window | Throughput-driven workloads |
| Cache layer (kv-cache) | 99.99% monthly | lookup < 5 ms | Cache is critical to reduce model cost |
| Control plane (model-router) | 99.9% monthly | API P95 < 200 ms | Configuration and routing must be highly available |

Error budget burn policy (standard tiers):
- Normal operation: track burn rate in dashboards and SLO channel.
- 25% burn: notify service owner and SRE.
- 50% burn: pause non-essential releases; begin weekly reliability review.
- 80% burn: escalate to oncall lead; require a mitigation plan within 24 hours.
- 100% burn: implement emergency measures (rollback, capacity increase, traffic tapering) until SLO is back in a healthy range.

SLO measurement windows and alerting:
- Primary window: rolling 28-day window for operational alerts and quarterly reporting.
- Secondary window: monthly calendar window for billing and contractual conversation.
- Alerts: two alert severities tied to error budget burn rate: SLO-BURN-WARN (25%/week) and SLO-BURN-CRIT (50%/24h). Configure alerts in PagerDuty with a dedicated SLO escalation policy.

Ownership and reviews:
- Service owners must document SLO definitions, SLIs sources, and dashboards in the service's Confluence page.
- Quarterly SLO review with SRE and product to validate thresholds and error budget allocations.

2) Capacity Planning Guidelines

Goals:
- Provision capacity to meet SLOs at target traffic percentiles while optimizing cost.
- Make capacity plans explicit, time-bounded, and reviewed by SRE and infra.

Inputs and assumptions:
- Traffic forecasts: 90/95/99 percentile traffic projections for next 3/6/12 months.
- Model performance profiles: tokens/sec, memory/KV cache requirements, peak GPU utilization per model variant (documented in model-catalog).
- Failure modes: capacity reserve for AZ failover and soft-degradation strategies (e.g., fallback to cheaper quantized variants).

Reserve policy (recommended):
- Normal growth: maintain 20% spare capacity headroom for burst absorption.
- Pre-planned launches or marketing events: run a dedicated capacity runbook and increase reserved capacity to 40% during the event window.
- For Dedicated customers with committed throughput, maintain capacity buffers aligned to SLA contracts (documented in the customer's infra runbook).

Calculation example (simple):
- Expected 95th percentile RPS = 500 req/s
- Average tokens per request = 50 tokens
- Average tokens/sec per GPU (model A) = 20k tokens/s
- GPUs required = ceil((500 * 50) / 20_000) = ceil(25_000/20_000) = 2 GPUs + buffer => 3 GPUs (with 20% headroom)

Autoscaling and burst policies:
- Use a hybrid autoscaler: fast-path (scale-up within 60s using spare warm pools) + slow-path (provision new nodes within 5-15 minutes).
- Warm pools: maintain a small pool of pre-warmed hosts per region to reduce cold-start latency for high-priority services.

Capacity planning cadence and deliverables:
- Monthly capacity forecast (SRE + infra) with 3/6/12 month projections.
- Pre-launch capacity checklist: traffic runbook, load-test sign-off, canary plan, rollback strategy, communication plan.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

Types of initiatives:
- Low-effort, high-impact fixes (e.g., circuit-breaker tuning, caching rules).
- Medium projects (e.g., auto-retry backoff improvements, KV cache sharding).
- Large investments (e.g., runtime kernel improvements, new batching algorithms).

Prioritization framework:
- Use RICE-like scoring factoring user impact, frequency (incidents/month), and cost to implement.
- Maintain a public reliability roadmap in eng-sre/roadmap and reserve 20% of sprint capacity for reliability work per team.

Implementation and measurement:
- Define success metrics (reduction in P95 latency, decrease in incident count, improved error budget headroom).
- Track initiatives as tickets with 'reliability:' label and require a short post-deployment validation plan.

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortems)

When to create a postmortem:
- Any SEV2/SEV1 incident impacting customer-facing SLOs or causing >1 hour of degraded service.
- Any full error budget exhaustion event.

Required postmortem sections (template):
- Summary: one-paragraph overview of what happened and impact.
- Timeline: chronological events with timestamps (UTC).
- Root cause analysis: clear RCA, not just symptoms.
- Detection & response: how the incident was detected and what mitigations were applied.
- Impact: customers, SLO burn, support tickets, and revenue/contract exposure if applicable.
- Corrective actions: short-term mitigations and long-term fixes with owners and target dates.
- Lessons learned and follow-ups: any changes to runbooks, alerts, or architecture.

Postmortem process:
1. Draft within 48 hours and publish as draft in Confluence.
2. Run a 60-minute incident review with SRE, service owners, and stakeholders within 7 days.
3. Finalize postmortem with assigned action items and due dates.
4. Track action item completion in the reliability board; actions older than 30 days require escalation.

5) Operational Tooling and Dashboards

Core tooling (minimum):
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex/Thanos for long-term retention.
- Tracing: Jaeger/OpenTelemetry (sampled with high-fidelity for errors).
- Logging: Structured logs in Datadog/Logstore with correlated request_id.
- Alerting: Datadog/Prometheus -> PagerDuty for oncall routing.
- Incident tracking: Jira with "incident" ticket type; link to Confluence postmortems.

Required dashboards and alerts per service:
- SLO dashboard (rolling 28d): availability, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), and error budget remaining.
- Capacity dashboard: GPU/host utilization, queue depth, warm-pool usage, scale events.
- Health checks and dependency map: upstream/downstream service status, degradation indicators.

Operational playbooks for common problems:
- High latency: check queue depth -> check KV cache hit rate -> check model GPU saturation -> rotate traffic to fallback model.
- High error rate: identify error class (4xx vs 5xx) -> check recent deploys -> roll back if correlation found.
- Low capacity / OOMs: drain new tasks, enable degraded mode (reduced concurrency), notify infra for emergency scale.

6) Runbook Templates and Examples

Runbook conventions:
- Each runbook must be compact (1-2 pages) with clear steps, commands, dashboards, and paging guidance.
- Include a short summary, impact indicators, quick triage checklist, mitigation steps, and escalation matrix.
- Keep runbooks under version control and reference the owning service and oncall rotation.

Example runbook: api-generation-high-tail-latency
- Summary: Significant increase in P99/P95 latency for api-generation impacting interactive latency.
- Indicators: SLO burn > 25% in 24h, P95 > 300ms, queue depth > 100 requests, GPU util > 85%.
- Quick triage:
  1) Check SLO dashboard and timeline.
  2) Evaluate recent deploys (last 60 minutes) in CI/CD.
  3) Check kv-cache hit rate and errors: dashboards/kv-cache-hits.
  4) Check batching behavior and queue sizes in batcher dashboard.
- Mitigation steps (ordered):
  1) Temporarily reduce concurrency by setting CONCURRENCY_OVERRIDE=0.6 via feature flag.
  2) Route a small percentage (5-10%) of traffic to fallback quantized model variant (model-A-q4_0) via model-router.
  3) If latency remains high, increase warm-pool allocation in affected region by +2 hosts.
  4) If errors increase or SLOs keep burning, execute rollback to previous deployment and notify customers.
- Post-incident: run memory and perf profiling, identify root cause, and add automated alerts for the observed metric changes.

Escalation matrix:
- Oncall engineer -> Service owner -> SRE lead -> Infrastructure oncall -> Eng manager (depending on severity and time of day).

7) Governance and Compliance

- Every production service must link this standards page and its own SLO documentation.
- SRE team will audit SLO coverage and runbook completeness quarterly.
- For customer-impacting outages, preserve audit logs and attach incident evidence to the postmortem (traces, screenshots, dashboards).

Appendices
A. Helpful CLI snippets:
- Check recent deploys: curl -sS "https://ci.redwood-inf/internal/api/deploys?service=api-generation&since=60m" | jq
- Query SLO burn (Prometheus):
  sum(rate(service_errors_total{service="api-generation"}[28d])) / sum(rate(service_requests_total{service="api-generation"}[28d]))

B. Useful dashboards and links:
- SLO dashboard: dashboards/slo/api-generation
- Capacity planning sheet: docs/capacity/2026-forecast
- Reliability board: boards/reliability

C. Contacts:
- SRE pager: #sre-pager (PagerDuty primary: SRE rotation)
- Infra ops: infra-oncall@redwood.com
- Incident commander rota: link confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotation

If you are a service owner and do not have a documented SLO, runbook, or capacity plan linked within 2 weeks of this publication, open a ticket with the reliability board and schedule a 30-minute onboarding review with SRE.
